column2: Unknown engine globals resolve to recording stubs
column3: A census over the 799 decompiled scripts found bare engine globals beyond the fixed prelude list (AppConfig 5 854 reads, FieldUtility 798, SoundController 796, engine classes such as CameraParameter 681); a `_G` metatable now returns a chainable recording stub on first read, so an event never hard-fails on an unported binding and the trace records the request

column2: Events run inside a Lua coroutine driven by a frame budget
column3: The engine resumes an event once per frame; the script's `stock.ScriptObjectHandle` delegates IsSkip/GetTargetID to the engine target (the binary registers `event_script::EventScriptObject` with exactly those two methods). The port builds that target (`host::make_event_target`) and drives `ScriptCall` in a coroutine whose body must be a Lua function (a Rust closure aborts the first yield across the C-call boundary). The reference event now runs to its field-system wait (`FieldObjectComponent.IsLoading`) instead of aborting at IsSkip
column4: drive events without a coroutine

column2: Flagwork sheets come from the update build
column3: The port runs the update code, so the tables it reads at runtime are the update ones: 450 event flags (vs 437 base), 45 event works (43), 70 map flags (64), 24 map works (4), 8 phase works (7), 704 system flags (561), 106 system works (96). column2: BNTX pixels decode through the Tegra block-linear layout
column3: The BRTI struct is the Wexos layout (width at +0x24, not +0x20 — that is the GPU access flag), the format is the GX2 table (0x2001 BC7_UNORM, 0x1d01 BC4, 0x1e01 BC5, 0x1c01 BC3, 0x2006 BC7_SRGB, 0x1f05 BC6_FLOAT, 0x0b01 RGBA8, 0x0201 R8), tile mode 0 = Tegra block-linear (deswizzled with tegra_swizzle), and blocks decode with bcdec_rs. Verified visually: pokeicon = a Pokemon egg icon (BC7, 79% transparent background), map frame (BC3), normal map (BC5, 127/128 endpoints), weather (BC4). Census of 2 969 update BNTX: BC7 1 823, BC4 541, BC7_SRGB 268, BC5 217, RGBA8 75, BC3 24, BC6 12, R8 1, unknown 8
column4: keep the raw-data-only parser

column2: The message `.dat` text encoding is still unidentified
column3: The `.tbl`/`.dat` addressing is cracked and verified (322/322 English files: header version/count/size/base 0x10, 8-byte entries {u32 offset, u16 length, u16 flags}, 4-byte aligned, last entry ends at the file end), but the code units are not plaintext (byte entropy ~7, no ASCII runs, no NUL high bytes) and the loader dispatches through an indirect call (FUN_00fc4f0c -> FUN_032a2370 -> `(*(code*)PTR_FUN_04270dc8)()`), so static analysis does not reach the decoder. The port exposes entries + raw units; decoded text is a follow-up
column4: guess a cipher

column2: The event-data chain is real; the flag is the event's own id
column3: `FindEventData(scriptID)` is a real binding now: it returns a table with the fields the scripts read (isFadeIn/isDemoSound/isResetPlayerLookAt/waitMotionType/statusReset/standUp/itemFadeOut, conservative defaults) and `__haxe_export_GetFlag` returning the script's own FnvHash64, so the script's `SetEventFlag(GetFlag())` lands in the real save system keyed by the event id. `bin/event/event_progress/event_list.bin` holds the real records (739 offsets, ~1 840 event names) but its layout is not decoded yet
column4: leave the chain as stubs

column2: FnvHash64 values are stored as exact bits in a signed Lua integer
column3: Lua 5.3 integers are signed, so a u64 above i64::MAX becomes a double and silently loses its low 11 bits (observed: the flag 0x83972a694a0579ee arrived as 0x83972a694a057800). The host stores `value` as `u64 as i64` and every consumer (__eq, __tostring, FnvHash64.new pass-through, SetEventFlag) reinterprets the bits as u64
column4: store the u64 directly

column2: The port's field is initialized, loaded and idle
column3: A headless port has no field to stream, so the field subsystem answers the events' wait conditions truthfully: FieldProc is initialized, the field object is not loading, the player stands (IsGrounded), nothing is riding and fades have finished. With that, the reference event runs end to end in one resume (ScriptCall returns 0 = success) instead of parking in a bounded 2 700-frame IsLoading loop
column4: synthesize fake progress

column2: The event_list.bin records are a nested offset graph; the name table is the usable layer
column3: The header is verified across three files (version 12/16, count, descending offset array: destination_list 0, event_result_sub_work 46, event_list 739) and the file carries a clean 1 821-entry name pool (length-prefixed identifiers, no overlaps: event names, FEVE_*/FSYS_* flags). The per-record fields hold signed relative offsets into further tables, so the record graph stays undecoded; the port exposes the name registry (hash -> name) and keeps the data fields at their defaults
column4: guess the record layout

column2: The two unknown BNTX formats are HDR float cubemaps, and ASTC is unused
column3: 0x1505 = R32_G32_FLOAT (8 B/px) and 0x1905 = R32_G32_B32_A32_FLOAT (16 B/px), both array_count 6 (probe cubemaps, values like 1.2685 or 0.0011); decoded with a clamped-linear tone map (face 0, mip 0). The format census over both builds finds no ASTC at all, so no ASTC decoder is needed
column4: implement ASTC anyway

column2: Message text: content-keyed deterministic encoding, algorithm still open
column3: Verified constraints: (1) the same plaintext yields the same ciphertext (one 5-unit string appears in 67 files); (2) not index-dependent (the same ciphertext appears at entry 0 and entry 1 of different files); (3) no duplicate ciphertexts within a file; (4) near-uniform byte output (entropy ~7.3) in both EN and JP; (5) not a fixed XOR against UTF-16 or UTF-8 English (shared-prefix test fails); (6) the loader dispatches indirectly (FUN_00fc4f0c -> FUN_032a2370 -> (*(code*)PTR_FUN_04270dc8)()) and the pointer's setter is outside the decompiled 12%. Next: decompile the setter or analyze subsdk0/subsdk1
column4: brute-force a cipher

column2: PARTLY CORRECTED by dec095/dec098 for trskl/tranm root/offset semantics: The tr* model family is a chunked container; parsing it is its own lane
column3: Census (update build): 3 748 files / 50.5 MB — .tranm 1 522 (19.5 MB), .trmbf 281 (25.7 MB mesh buffers), .trmsh 281, .trmdl 253, .trmtr 253, .trskl 199, plus camera/animation clip variants. Verified: the first u32 is a per-type header size (trmdl 24, trskl 16, trmbf 12, tranm 12/4 — constant across every file of the type), followed by small u16/u32 counts and a u16 section-offset table (Game Freak's chunked style, like the message .dat family). A full parser is a multi-session RE task and the port's renderer needs meshes before physics or animation, so it is a follow-up lane
column4: parse it now

column2: Havok stays deferred; the approach is baking colliders, not emulating Havok
column3: The 80 .hkx files (2.4 MB) are the standard tagged binary (TAG0 | SDKV20200200 | DATA); they are collision/physics data for characters and props. The port has no gameplay simulation yet, so nothing needs colliders: avian3d integration waits until a system does, and the approach then is baking colliders from the .hkx offline rather than emulating Havok at runtime
column4: emulate Havok

column2: The message decoder is not in main.elf
column3: Ghidra xref search over the whole program (ExportXrefs.java, new tool): address 0x04270dc8 (the pointer behind the message loader's indirect call) has exactly one reference — the thunk itself — and is never written in main.elf. The callback is therefore registered from another ExeFS module (subsdk0/subsdk1/rtld) or through a relocation table. Next step for the text cipher: analyze those modules with Ghidra (they are extracted but not yet imported)
column4: keep searching main.elf

column2: Message text is XORed with a per-index 16-byte repeating key (cracked)
column3: plain_char[p] = ciphertext[2p] XOR key[p % 16], one 16-byte key per entry index (the per-position keystream repeats every 16 bytes; the per-index keys also overlap each other with a shift). Characters live in the even bytes, 0x00 terminates. Keys recovered by frequency analysis pooling every position p = j (mod 16): .tools/message_cipher.py writes them outside the repo (game-derived). Wired into the port: assets/message.rs MessageKeystream + the message subsystem's __port_load_messages / GetMessage / SetMessage (returns the decoded text) / IsEndMessage; the window state follows the message (open while pending, closed by CloseMessageWindow). Fixture test decodes str_pocketname_005 = 'Everyday Items' through the host. Evidence: one 5-char string appears at index 0 of 67 files and no ciphertext ever appears at two different indices; the high byte of each unit is constant per position across ~300 files with only +-0x20 (ASCII case) variants, which pins the keystream shape. Recovered with frequency analysis plus a seeded index 0 (known plaintext 'Survey Report:' from advresult.dat): decoded output reads 'Pokemon Ball' names, 'None', 'n/a', 'Money', 'Satchel', 'Yes', 'The next day...', 'Now saving...' and full sentences with control codes (0x10 0x02 tags, 0x00 NUL). Tool: .tools/message_cipher.py. Remaining: the first 1-2 positions of each index need seeding (short strings starve the frequency attack)
column4: keep brute-forcing

column2: PARTLY CORRECTED by dec095/dec098 for trskl/tranm root/offset semantics: tr* container: per-type header size + offset tables + name references
column3: Verified on real files: the first u32 is the header size, constant per type (trmdl 24, trskl 16, trmbf/trmtr/tranm 12) but NOT a universal layout beyond that — the following u16s differ per type (trmdl u16 0/18; trskl 12/16; trmbf 8/8; tranm 8/12) and even per file within .tranm. Inside a .trmdl (240 B sample, fully dumped): a u32 offset table at 0x1C ([0x9c, 0x70, 0x44, 0x3c]), transform floats at 0x3C (0x40a83028...), and length-prefixed filename references at 0x70 ('gimmick_atrtest_01.trmtr') and 0x9C ('gimmick_atrtest_01.trskl') — a model descriptor points at its material and skeleton by name, and the mesh data lives in .trmbf/.trmsh. Parser is the next work unit; the census (3748 files / 50.5 MB) and the per-type header sizes are the starting point
column4: parse it blind

column2: A .trmbf mesh buffer = vertex block at 0x44 + u16 triangle indices
column3: Verified on two files (1 428 B and 10 128 B): the u32 at 0x28 is the vertex-block size, the block starts at 0x44, and the rest of the file is a u16 index buffer — its length is a multiple of 3 and every index stays below the vertex count (sample: 72 indices / 24 triangles; big file: 1 092 indices / 364 triangles, max index 217). assets/tr.rs parses that (TrMbf: vertex block + indices). The vertex stride and attribute layout are still open (the block does not divide evenly by 12/16/24), so the port exposes the raw block until the attribute descriptors are decoded
column4: guess the stride

column2: The geometry chain is .trmdl -> .trmsh -> .trmbf
column3: A .trmsh is the mesh descriptor: it carries length-prefixed references to its .trmbf (the vertex/index buffers), a 'mesh' tag and a per-submesh name ('gimmick_atrtest_01_01'), plus nested tables of u16/u32 counts and offsets (sample: u16 0x1e with u32 0x16c/0x14c). That is the lead for the vertex attribute layout: the submesh entries hold the counts, and the .trmbf header fields (8, 8, 4, 12, 1, 4, 8 at 0x04..0x24) are the candidate attribute descriptors — the block does not divide evenly by 12/16/24, so the attributes are likely several concatenated arrays rather than one interleaved stride. Next session: dump a .trmsh submesh entry against its .trmbf to solve the stride
column4: guess the stride

column2: The .trmbf vertex block is not a single interleaved array
column3: Decisive test: the block sizes do not admit one stride. Small file: 1216 bytes, max index 32 (>= 33 verts) -> strides 4/8/16/32/64 divide it (16 -> 76 verts, 32 -> 38 verts); big file: 7876 bytes, max index 217 (>= 218 verts) -> only 4 and 44 divide it, and 44 gives 179 verts < 218, so it is ruled out. A single stride therefore cannot describe both files, which means the block holds several concatenated attribute arrays (positions, normals, UVs, skin data) rather than one interleaved layout. Next step: decode the per-array descriptors — the 56 bytes between the .trmbf header (12) and the vertex data (0x44) are the prime candidate (14 u32s: 8, 4, 1, 12, 0x000c0008, 0x00080004, 8, 1216, 4, 1, 4, -1210, 4, 1188), cross-checked against the .trmsh submesh entries
column4: assume one stride

column2: The .trmbf vertex stride is 36 bytes
column3: Solved exactly on both verified files: the u32 at 0x40 is the vertex data size, and dividing it by 36 gives the vertex count the indices need — 1 188/36 = 33 (max index 32) and 7 848/36 = 218 (max index 217). The vertex block (u32 at 0x28) carries a 28-byte prefix, so the vertices start at 0x60 and the u16 indices follow the block at 0x44 + size. TrMbf now exposes stride/count and rejects a file whose indices fall outside the count. The per-attribute split inside the 36 bytes (likely position 12 + normal 12 + UV 8 + 4) is the remaining detail
column4: keep guessing the stride

column2: The 36-byte vertex is not the classic position/normal/UV layout
column3: Column analysis on a real item mesh (item_228, 2 728 verts): the three 12-byte groups inside each record are statistically near-identical (each group's first two floats span 0..1, its third spans -1.6..0, ~270 distinct values), and in each record exactly one group carries the large values while the others stay near zero. A stride-12 read of the same block gives three arrays with the same ranges and growing average lengths (0.24 / 0.38 / 0.50) — so this is not (position, normal, UV) interleaved. The values look like texture-space basis data (tangent/bitangent pairs with a signed component). Next step: find the attribute descriptors in the game code (the mesh loader) or correlate a mesh against its rendered look
column4: keep guessing the split

column2: The mesh loader is not in the decompiled 18%%
column3: Search for the attribute descriptors: no function in the decompiled set references the 'trmbf' string — the only .trmdl references are path tables (FUN_01b0f6e4 is a model registry). The mesh loader therefore sits in the un-decompiled 82%% of main.elf or in another ExeFS module. Next session: rank the triage around the model/mesh subsystem and export that tranche, or import the ExeFS modules
column4: keep searching the same set

column2: The ExeFS modules do not carry the mesh attribute names either
column3: subsdk1 contains POSITION / texcoordH / color.back, but the surrounding strings are CUDA/NVCC runtime internals (fragment.attrib[%d], .threadgemask, dlayer, __cuda_sm70_votesync_), and subsdk0/sdk only show colour/position words from unrelated libraries. No trmbf/trmsh/trmdl reference in any ExeFS module. So the attribute semantics are neither in the decompiled main.elf nor in the SDK modules: the remaining leads are a deeper main.elf tranche, a mesh-vs-render correlation, or accepting the 36-byte record as opaque basis data for now
column4: keep string-searching

column2: The vertex count is max(index)+1 and the stride is derived from it
column3: Every vertex of a mesh is referenced, so the count comes from the indices and the stride is u32@0x40 / count — an exact integer on every verified file: 33 verts/stride 36, 218/36, 120/36, 71/36, 275/36, 157/36, 93/36, 474/36 (gimmick models) and 2 046 verts/stride **48** (item_228). The stride therefore varies per file with the attribute set, which corrects dec051's fixed 36. TrMbf derives both, validates the divisibility and a plausible stride range, and the fixture test keeps 33/36
column4: assume one stride

column2: The render path works: BNTX -> decode -> Bevy sprite -> window
column3: Solved with a windowed spike (examples/window_spike.rs): a real BNTX (pokeicon, 512x512 BC7) decodes to RGBA8, uploads as a Bevy Image and draws as a sprite in a Vulkan window (RTX 4060); the screenshot shows the egg icon. The blocker was not the render app but the feature set: Bevy 0.19 splits bevy_sprite (logic) from **bevy_sprite_render** (render), and without the latter sprites never reach the GPU even though the clear colour renders. Cargo features now include bevy_winit/x11/wayland/bevy_state/png/bevy_sprite_render; the example screenshots and exits so it can be verified without a human watching
column4: leave it headless

column2: The mesh path does not render yet (sprite path does)
column3: mesh_spike.rs builds a Bevy Mesh from a real .trmbf (positions from one 12-byte group per record, normalised, u16 indices -> u32), spawns Mesh3d + an unlit StandardMaterial and a Camera3d, and screenshots at frame 45; every run returns the clear colour only. The sprite path in window_spike.rs renders the same decoded texture fine, so the difference is 3D-specific: bevy_pbr is enabled and the 3D types compile, which leaves the candidates as the capture timing versus pipeline compilation, a missing 3D plugin/feature (bevy_pbr may need its own render half like bevy_sprite_render did), or the mesh data itself. Isolation done: a procedural triangle renders in the same app (3/4 camera), so the 3D scene, camera, material and pipeline all work; the trmbf model does not appear. Its geometry is valid (0/24 degenerate triangles with group 0 positions, bbox x,y in 0..1 and z in -3.7..3.7 before normalisation) and every attribute group has finite values, so the remaining suspect is how the model's Mesh is built/uploaded rather than the data or the scene. Point-cloud test done: the mesh render path WORKS — the point cloud draws (green points) and the indexed mesh draws too, as a thin vertical strip for group 0; group 2 is fully degenerate (24/24 zero-area triangles). So the Bevy mesh/asset/material/indices path is fine and the 'invisible model' was a sliver, but **none of the three interleaved 12-byte groups is the position**. That revives the concatenated-arrays hypothesis with concrete numbers: item_228's block 98 208 = 3 x 32 736, i.e. three arrays of 2 046 x 16 bytes (the gimmick's 1 188 = 3 x 396 = three arrays of 33 x 12). Tested the concatenated-arrays reading: item_228's block splits into three 32 736-byte parts (2 046 x 16) whose per-column ranges are nearly IDENTICAL (x 0..0.98, z +-0.008, w +-0.018; only the second column's negative extent grows -0.57/-1.11/-1.61), so they are not three attribute arrays but three views of the same kind of data. A u16/s16 re-read of the 48-byte record shows no quantised positions either (the wide lanes are just float high halves). So the vertex payload looks like texture-space basis data throughout and the position is not in the vertex block as read; the next leads are a different vertex-block offset (the 28-byte prefix is a candidate) or the mesh loader in a deeper tranche. The render path itself is proven (a point cloud and the indexed mesh both draw). Two further findings: the block reads as four concatenated 12-byte arrays (98 208 = 4 x 2 046 x 12, exact), and the spike's normalised bbox for array 0 is x ~0, y 0..1, z -0.40..0.002, i.e. a flat y-z plane that every camera angle showed edge-on or not at all. Unexplained and unresolved: Python reads the first floats at 0x60 as (0.733, 0.787, ~0) while the spike's bbox says x ~0 for all vertices, so the two disagree about the same bytes; the next session should print the first raw positions inside the spike to find that discrepancy before trusting either
column4: keep assuming the interleaved layout

column2: SUPERSEDED by dec063: the block is not concatenated arrays
column3: Wrong reading. The concatenated split only looked plausible because reading the first 24552 bytes of a packed 48-byte record mixes positions with other attributes. dec063 found the true layout with a systematic search (position at floats 0, 1, 5) and dec067 showed it varies per model. Kept for the record of what was ruled out.
column4: treat the block as concatenated arrays

column2: Array 0 is the position; the other arrays are not normals
column3: With the correct array offsets (0x60 + k x count x 12) item_228 shows array 0 = (0.733, 0.787, 0.0) with x,y in 0..0.98 and z in -0.10..0.01 (the position that renders the model) and arrays 1..3 with the same x,y ranges but growing negative z extents (-0.5, -0.88, -1.28). No array is unit-length (0.03-0.07 unit-like), so none is a normal, and the values are not 0..1 UVs either. They look like further per-vertex attributes with a similar encoding; the mesh loader (a deeper Ghidra tranche) or a UV check in the renderer would disambiguate
column4: keep guessing

column2: SUPERSEDED by dec063/dec067: the arrays are not independent vertex sets
column3: Wrong reading, same root cause as dec058. With the packed record (position at floats 0, 1, 5) the "independent vertex sets" were an artefact of slicing 48-byte records at 24552-byte boundaries. What is still true and useful: array 1 rendered as positions draws a coherent shape, and no array is a normal.
column4: treat them as separate meshes

column2: PARTLY SUPERSEDED by dec067: the .trmsh declares the attribute table, not shapes
column3: The .trmsh does reference the .trmbf and declare the index count (3 564, exact), and it names chain_mesh and chain_mesh_shape. But the "shape keys" conclusion came from the wrong array reading (dec058/dec060). What dec067 later showed: the .trmsh carries the per-model attribute table (11 twelve-byte entries) which is where the attribute semantics must come from.
column4: treat the extra arrays as shape keys

column2: The .trmtr is a property list that names the textures by role
column3: item_228.trmtr (1 604 B) is a flat NUL-terminated property list: the texture entries are a *.bntx file name followed by its role (item_228_obj_alb.bntx/BaseColorMap, _nrm/NormalMap, _rgn/RoughnessMap, _mtl/MetallicMap, _ao/AOMap) plus flags (EnableBaseColorMap, EnableAlphaTest, ...). TrMtr::parse extracts them and base_color() picks the albedo; the spike loads and decodes it (256 x 256) as the mesh's base_color_texture
column4: keep the material opaque

column2: CORRECTED by dec092: item position is ID 1 at byte offsets 0/4/8
column3: The earlier float-triple candidate (0, 1, 5) is superseded by the `.trmsh` declaration. A systematic search over all 220 float triples of the 48-byte record leaves (0, 1, 5) as the only candidate with volume on every axis (0.96 x 0.96 x 1.61) and short uniform edges; rendering it draws a dense coherent surface. Floats 2..4 are integers (they read as denormals, 11 distinct byte patterns) and 6..11 are quantized small values (normals/tangents), so the block is not a plain float array. TrMbf::position reads (0, 1, 5)
column4: the block is a float array

column2: CORRECTED by dec077: the block is not two identical halves
column3: The 3 564 indices are an exact quad pattern — (0,1,2)(2,1,3), (4,5,6)(6,5,7), ... — 1 188 triangles over 2 046 vertices, and with the (0,1,5) positions the triangle edges are p50 0.145 / p90 0.217 / p99 0.278 with only 2 outliers above 0.3. WRONG on one point: the block is NOT two identical 49104-byte halves. What holds is the quad index pattern and the edge statistics. dec077 measured 29 203 differing bytes between the halves
column4: treat the halves as identical

column2: Bevy 0.19 splits bevy_light and needs tonemapping_luts, or the render is magenta
column3: Two missing cargo features made every lit render come out flat magenta: without `bevy_light` the scene has no light types at all, and without `tonemapping_luts` (which pulls `zstd_rust` for the KTX2 LUTs) Bevy logs 'TonyMcMapFace tonemapping requires the tonemapping_luts feature' and the shader samples a missing LUT. With both features the mesh renders lit and textured with the game's own albedo (the brown 154,74,70 texture). Same class of bug as bevy_sprite_render (dec056): a split crate silently degrades the render instead of failing
column4: keep the default feature set

column2: The .trmtr flags parse value-first and drive the material
column3: The boolean properties are written value-before-name (`True | EnableBaseColorMap`), so TrMtr pairs each True/False string with the following Enable* name. The spike honours them: EnableBaseColorMap/EnableNormalMap/EnableRoughnessMap/EnableMetallicMap/EnableAOMap decide which maps load (roughness and metallic are packed into Bevy's single metallic-roughness texture, G/B) and EnableAlphaTest switches alpha_mode to Mask(0.5). No normals ship in the vertex data (no byte offset yields unit vectors), so the spike derives them from the geometry with compute_normals()
column4: assume the flags are name-first

column2: CORRECTED by dec092: ID 6 stores UV0; rock LOD1 has 200 vertices
column3: The 329-vertex rock count and no-UV conclusion were based on the wrong payload boundary/alignment; item and cliff positions are also ID 1 at bytes 0/4/8. Quantitative UV oracle: a correct UV map keeps the texel density (3D triangle area / UV area) near-constant across triangles, so its coefficient of variation is low. Scanning every byte offset of the record for f32 pairs, u16 pairs (raw and biased), s16 pairs, 10-10 / 11-11 bit-packing and byte pairs leaves the best CV at 1.32 against the ~0.3 a real unwrap shows, and no offset works across models. The layout is also per-model: d110_gimmick_rock02 (329 verts, 11 844 = 329 x 36) puts the position at floats (0,1,2) with extents 0.99 x 0.995 x 2.37, while item_228 (2046 verts, 98 208 = 2046 x 48) needs (0,1,5) — its edge coherence is 0.1185 against 0.478 for the best stride-36 reading. The per-model attribute table is in the .trmsh (item_228 declares 11 twelve-byte entries and the index count 3 564), so that is where the attribute semantics must come from
column4: keep searching the vertex record

column2: The .trmsh ends in a fixed attribute-descriptor table shared across models
column3: Both d110_gimmick_rock02_lod1.trmsh (524 B) and item_228.trmsh (688 B) end in a byte-identical block: a chain of entries each with a u32 that looks like a name hash (0x2b, 0x2b, 0x33) followed by the classic Nintendo u16 field-offset tables (0e 00 16 00 04 00 08 00 00 00 0c 00 10 00 0e 00 = 14, 22, 4, 8, 0, 12, 16, 14), plus relative name offsets (-98, -78, -22) and counts (39, 22, 36). Because two unrelated models share it byte for byte, it is a fixed vertex-layout signature: the attribute list with its formats. It is the concrete, bounded place where the attribute semantics (and therefore where the UVs live in a record) must be read from; the rest of the .trmsh is per-model (the .trmbf name, the sub-mesh names chain_mesh / chain_mesh_shape / gimmick_rock02_lod1_mesh1, the index count 3 564 / 380 / 348 and the model bounds as floats)
column4: decode the vertex record by hand

column2: CORRECTED by dec092: `.trmsh` ID 1 is authoritative; triangle-quality inference is fallback only
column3: The heuristic is retained only for `.trmbf` files without a valid sibling layout; the three references use ID 1 at byte offsets 0/4/8. Since the layout varies per model (dec067), TrMbf::detect_position searches the record's float triples and keeps the one that maximises triangle quality (area / longest edge squared) among triples with volume on every axis. Quality is the right criterion: a wrong triple turns the mesh into slivers (exactly the spikes the renders showed) and drives the score to zero, and unlike raw edge length it is independent of the triple's scale — the naive edge test picked item_228's tiny quantised (0, 5, 7) and the rock's degenerate (5, 7, 8). Results: item_228 resolves decisively to (0, 1, 5) at 0.230 against 0.090 for the runner-up (2.5x), while the rock stays ambiguous (1, 2, 4 = 0.147 vs 0, 1, 2 = 0.125) because its record carries near-duplicate channels — its block, like the item's, is two equal halves (11 844 = 2 x 329 x 18), which points at a half-length record with a repeated half
column4: assume one layout for every model

column2: The .trmsh tail is the shader input layout, not per-model data
column3: The byte-identical block that closes both .trmsh files parses as three entries with a descending index (3, 2, 1), a u32 (43, 43, 51) and Nintendo u16 field-offset tables whose values (0, 4, 8, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22, 28) are the field offsets of a fixed structure — the shape of a Direct3D-style input-element description (semantic, index, format, slot, aligned byte offset, classification, step rate). FNV-1a and FNV-1 hashes of the obvious attribute names (p0, position, normal, uv0, texcoord0, ...) match neither 43 nor 51, and because two unrelated models share the block byte for byte it cannot be per-model geometry: it is the vertex-input signature the mesh is bound to. That is consistent with the layout varying per model (dec067/dec069) while the shader stays fixed, and it means the UV location must be read from the format fields, not from the model
column4: decode it as a name table

column2: IBL: Bevy 0.19 needs a stacked image, and an sRGB cubemap kills the render
column3: Attempting EnvironmentMapLight exposed two concrete facts. (1) Image::reinterpret_stacked_2d_as_array does not build a cubemap from six independent faces: it slices the HEIGHT of a depth-1 image into layers, so the image must be created as (width, height x layers, 1) and reinterpreting a (w, h, 6) descriptor returns InvalidLayerCount. Image::new also asserts pixel_count(size) * pixel_size == data.len(), so passing six faces into a depth-1 descriptor panics with 'Pixel data, size and format have to match'. (2) With the cubemap built that way the app then exits without producing the screenshot and without a logged error, so the Rgba8UnormSrgb cubemap is not a usable environment map: the next attempt must use Rgba16Float (what Bevy's own HDR probes use) and log the render error instead of relying on the screenshot. The spike was reverted to the committed version so the working render stays green
column4: keep trying sRGB cubemaps

column2: IBL works: HDR cubemap + a Cube view descriptor
column3: EnvironmentMapLight renders once three things line up: (1) the image is built as (width, height x 6, 1) and reinterpret_stacked_2d_as_array(6) slices the height into layers; (2) the format is Rgba16Float, written through a small f32 -> f16 converter so the spike needs no new dependency; and (3) the image carries texture_view_descriptor = TextureViewDescriptor { dimension: Some(Cube) }, because the lighting bind group wants a cube view and a plain D2 array fails validation with 'BindGroup with mesh_view_bind_group_binding_array label is invalid'. Surfacing the render error (RUST_LOG) instead of relying on the screenshot is what found the third point. With it the metallic surface reflects the sky instead of rendering black, and the model reads as lit rather than dark
column4: keep the D2 array view

column2: The shaders ship with the game and carry the attribute semantics
column3: The .trmtr's 'Standard' string resolves to a real shader: system_resource/gfx2/shader/env/material/ holds 70 files (22 MB) of *.bnsh (42, compiled shaders) and *.trsha (27, shader configs) plus one trtch, with the material set ha_standard, ha_unlit, ha_transparent, ha_water, ha_fabric, ha_non_directional, ha_effect, ha_eye and more. ha_standard.trsha (22 912 B) lists exactly the property schema the .trmtr instances fill in — EnableBaseColorMap, EnableNormalMap, EnableAlphaMap, EnableAlphaTest, NumMaterialLayer, InstancedType, EnableVertexBaseColor — plus NumRequiredUV, the count of UVs the shader requires, and it names its binary (ha_standard.bnsh, 11.6 MB, 'BNSH' magic, version bytes 0b 01 02 00) and its shader entry point (haStandard). The .bnsh body is compressed or opaque GPU bytecode (no readable strings, no zlib stream at the usual offsets), so the vertex input signature has to be read from that container. This closes the direction of #1: the attribute semantics are not in the mesh at all — they belong to the shader the mesh is bound to, which is exactly why the .trmsh tail is identical across models
column4: read the semantics out of the mesh file

column2: The shader names every vertex attribute: the UVs are attributes 5 and 7
column3: The .bnsh is not opaque: it embeds its programs as readable NVN assembly (!!NVvp5.0 vertex, !!NVfp5.0 fragment, 720 programs), so the vertex input semantics come straight from the game. ha_standard's vertex program declares ATTRIB vertex_attrib[] = { vertex.attrib[0..5] } (and 0..7 in the variant with a second UV set) and uses them unambiguously: MOV.F R3.xyz, vertex.attrib[0] feeds DP4 result.position — so 0 is the POSITION; vertex.attrib[1] is used with DP3 against the basis vectors and becomes result.attrib[2].xyz — the NORMAL; vertex.attrib[3] gets the same DP3 treatment plus MOV result.attrib[3].w, vertex.attrib[3] — the TANGENT with its w handedness; and MOV.F result.attrib[0].xy, vertex.attrib[5] passes attribute 5 straight through as the first texture coordinate, with vertex.attrib[7] going to result.attrib[0].zw as the second. So the UVs are attributes 5 and 7 of the vertex, not a float pair hidden in the record, and the record must carry all of them — which is why the earlier texel-density search over float pairs could never find one
column4: keep looking for a float pair in the record

column2: SUPERSEDED by dec092: item position is ID 1 at bytes 0/4/8, not two 24-byte streams
column3: The two-stream interpretation was inferred from the wrong float alignment; the `.trmsh` descriptor and bounds confirm ID 1 at byte offsets 0/4/8. With the shader semantics known (dec074), item_228's verified position reading (0, 1, 5) stops being odd: x and y sit at the start of the record and z twenty bytes later, which is the signature of two interleaved streams. Stream A (bytes 0..23) carries the position; stream B (24..47) carries the remaining attributes, and its varying bytes (24..37) hold the packed normal/tangent/UV data — floats that read as 1e-3..1e-5, i.e. quantised rather than plain float. Testing stream B for a UV pair leaves the texel-density CV above 2.0 for every u16 offset, and the earlier full-record sweep already excluded f32, u16 (raw and biased), s16, byte pairs and 10-10 / 11-11 bit-packing, so the mapping from the shader's attribute indices (0..7) to record byte offsets is still missing: it must come from the input-layout declaration, which is the .trmsh tail whose format fields are still opaque (dec070). The shader gives the semantics; the layout gives the offsets, and only the first is decoded
column4: keep guessing the byte offsets

column2: The .trmbf header is a fixed structure with Nintendo field-offset tables
column3: The 68-byte header that precedes the vertex block is byte-identical in shape across models (item_228 and d110_gimmick_rock02_lod1 share every field, only the sizes differ): two copies of a Nintendo field-offset structure (u16 runs 8, 8, 0, 4, 8, 0 and 8, 12, 4, 8, 8, 0) built around the sizes 12, 8 and 4 — three, two and one float — followed by the block size at 0x28, its negation at 0x38 and the vertex byte count at 0x40. That is the shape of a buffer/attribute declaration, but the attribute byte offsets still do not fall out of it: reading f32 pairs at every offset the header suggests (8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36) gives either a degenerate range or a texel-density CV of 3.3 or worse, against the ~0.3 a real unwrap shows. So the record's UV bytes stay undecoded under f32, u16 (raw and biased), s16, byte, half-float and 10-10 / 11-11 encodings at every byte offset. The remaining path is the header's field tables themselves, whose schema lives in the engine rather than the data
column4: read the offsets out of the header

column2: Correcting dec064: the block halves differ, and the 24-byte reading alternates
column3: Re-measuring the two 49104-byte halves of item_228's vertex block shows 29 203 differing bytes, not zero: dec064's 'two identical halves' was wrong (the equality it rested on compared 24552-byte windows at a 49104-byte offset, which is a different claim). Reading the block as 24-byte records is also self-consistent but alternates: even records carry real positions (x, y in 0..1, z negative) while odd records carry x = 0 and y = +/-0.018 with z = 0.0078 — exactly the model bounds the .trmsh declares (0.0078 and 0.0181), so the odd records are not free-floating junk. The packed 12 bytes at offsets 8..19 do vary (18 distinct values at 8..11, 102 at 16..19, with 14..15 constant), which kills the earlier 'constant padding' reading, and neither a u16 pair nor an s16 triple in that region passes the UV or normal tests
column4: keep the 48-byte reading

column2: CORRECTED by dec093: ID 6 stores UV0; the prior byte-alignment sweep missed it
column3: The UV-negative search used the wrong byte alignment; verified ID 6 is two f32 values at offset 28 and matches shader UV0 evidence (dec074). The .trmtr declares UVScaleOffset, whose name covers both a scale and an offset: reading a single f32 immediately before the name returns a denormal (1.8e-38), so the property is a vector (scale.xy + offset.xy) and the scalar read is only kept when it lands in a plausible range. That matters because it is the last piece of evidence for where the UVs come from: every encoding of a UV pair in the record is now excluded — f32, u16 raw and biased, s16, byte pairs, half-floats (tested in the odd records, where 00 3c decodes as exactly 1.0 and made the lead look promising), 10-10 and 11-11 bit-packing — at every byte offset, in both the 48-byte and 24-byte readings, and the texel-density oracle rejects them all. Combined with a material that carries a UV transform and a mesh that carries none, the reading is that the game projects the UVs and the material transforms them, which is why the spike's planar projection already looks close
column4: assume the UVs are a packed pair

column2: The material roles are enumerated and the maps are wired
column3: Scanning 253 .trmtr files gives the full role list: BaseColorMap 257, NormalMap 220, RoughnessMap 183, AOMap 181, MetallicMap 108, PackedMap 35, WeatherLayerMaskMap 15, NormalMap1 12, BaseColorMap1 9, EmissionColorMap 7, WindMaskMap 5, FoamMaskMap 3, FlowMap 3, NormalMap2 3. Two of them map straight onto Bevy: PackedMap is the game's ARM map (R = AO, G = roughness, B = metallic), which is exactly StandardMaterial's metallic-roughness layout, so it feeds metallic_roughness_texture and occlusion_texture at once; and EmissionColorMap feeds emissive_texture with the material's EmissionColor as the tint (enabled by EnableEmissionColorMap, which item_001 has False and item_224 has True). WeatherLayerMaskMap has no Bevy counterpart because the layer textures come from the global weather system, so it is reported only. Two robustness findings came out of testing this: item_224 ships 8 158 indices, not a multiple of three, so the parser now keeps the complete triangles instead of rejecting the file, and its header does not follow the same field layout as item_228/rock (the value at 0x28 reads as a negative block size), so it is a second .trmbf variant to map
column4: assume one header layout

column2: The second .trmbf variant is multi-buffer and is rejected cleanly
column3: item_224 does not follow the single-buffer header: its field at 0x14 reads 5 where item_228 reads 1, followed by five values (14528, 6808, 5720, 2376, 1948) and two negative relative offsets (-14500, -16066), so the file holds several buffers (its .trmtr names two objects, obj01 and obj02) and the field at 0x28/0x40 is not a vertex-block size. A generic split search over the file, keeping only splits whose index buffer is complete and whose vertex block divides into a stride between 12 and 64, finds no candidate for it (the only arithmetically possible split implies stride 504), so the file is a genuinely different layout rather than a shifted one. The port now reports it as unsupported and the spike exits cleanly instead of panicking, so a layout it cannot read never takes the process down; item_228 still parses and renders unchanged
column4: assume every .trmbf is single-buffer

column2: The .trmbf is a multi-mesh container and both variants now parse
column3: item_224 is not a shifted single-buffer file: it is a container. Scanning for runs of plausible positions (finite, bounded, not all zero, 12-byte stride) finds eight vertex runs of 160, 72, 256, 67, 83, 44, 39 and 27 vertices, each followed by a short descriptor and then its own index buffer, and the header's five values (14528, 6808, 5720, 2376, 1948) are offsets to those buffers rather than sizes. The 65535 sentinel that appears in each index buffer marks the end of its run. The parser now falls back to a container walk when the header does not describe one block: it finds the first vertex run, skips the descriptor, and keeps the index buffer that follows, so item_224 loads as 158 vertices and 66 triangles and renders with its albedo, while item_228 still reads as 2 046 vertices and 1 188 triangles. Every model family in the port now parses
column4: assume every .trmbf is single-buffer

column2: CORRECTED by dec092: cliff position is ID 1 at bytes 0/4/8; its count remains 1,155
column3: The cliff's prior (3, 4, 5) position result used the wrong payload start; the confirmed `.trmsh` bounds match byte offsets 0/4/8 within a 0.004 margin. The stride check was the last blocker for the third family: field pack models such as ground_area02_cliff01 declare 46 200 vertex bytes for 1 155 vertices, a stride of 40, which is not a multiple of twelve and was rejected even though the count is right. The rule is now the correct one — the stride only has to divide the block evenly and stay between 12 and 64 — and detect_position finds where the position sits inside the record (floats 3, 4 and 5 there against 0, 1 and 5 on item_228). So the port reads three families: single-buffer items (item_228, 2 046 verts / 1 188 tris), multi-mesh containers (item_224, 158 verts / 66 tris) and field terrain (ground_area02_cliff01, 1 155 verts / 2 101 tris), each rendering with its own albedo. UVScaleOffset is a single scale followed by padding — (1, 0, 0, 0) in every material seen — so a zero second component applies the scale to both axes, and the layer maps (BaseColorMap1, LayerMaskMap) load alongside the first
column4: require a stride that is a multiple of twelve

column2: Layer blending is implemented; the mask source is the vertex colour
column3: The CPU blend is in place: when a material declares both BaseColorMap1 and LayerMaskMap the spike composes the two albedos through the mask and hands Bevy a single texture. No material in the game has both, and the reason is in the .trsha: LayerMaskSource is one of VertexColor, Texture or Const, so the layered materials (BaseColorMap1, 9 of 253) take their mask from the vertex colour, gated by EnableVertexBaseColor. That puts the layer blend behind the same blocker as the UVs — the vertex attributes are named by the shader (0 position, 1 normal, 3 tangent, 5 UV0, 7 UV1, with the colour among the unused ones) but their byte offsets inside the record are still unmapped. TrMbf::parse_all now returns every mesh of a container instead of only the first, so a caller can take one mesh or the whole model
column4: assume a mask texture always exists

column2: The input-layout declaration is a Nintendo field-offset structure whose schema is not self-describing
column3: Following the last lead: the .trmsh ends in four entries of the shape [u16 id][u16 pad][u16 field offsets...] with the ids 3, 2, 1 and 51 (0x33) and offsets such as 8, 28, 4, 16, 8, 0 — all below their leading value, which is what makes 43 (0x2B) and 51 read as structure sizes or type codes rather than names. Its head carries the classic Nintendo u16 offset tables (u16 runs at a four-byte step: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 then 24, 40, 44, 48) plus two per-model values that differ by exactly 32 in every file measured (rock 380/348, item_228 572/540, field cliff 388/356), so those two are an offset/length pair rather than two independent counts. The shape is mapped but the schema is not: which field is the stride, which is the attribute offset and which is a name reference lives in the engine's loader, not in the file, and the .bnsh cannot help either because the vertex input signature is declared by the application through NVN rather than stored in the shader. So the remaining step for the attribute offsets is a Ghidra tranche over the loader (the decompiled set covers about 20%), not more byte archaeology: three models across three families give a consistent structure to validate any candidate against, and the port already reads all of them without it
column4: read the semantics out of the structures

column2: The per-model part of the .trmsh carries per-model numbers, but they do not close the schema
column3: The .trmsh has a per-model head and an identical tail (dec070). The head does hold per-model numbers: after the .trmbf name and a fixed run (1, 36, 1966080, 262196, 786440, 1310736, 0, 0, 2621464, 3145772, 30) every file carries its own pair that differs by exactly 32 (item_228 572/540, rock 380/348, field 388/356), its own pair further down (284/232, 140/72, 124/48) and its own triple ending in 4 (32/24/4, 48/40/4, 24/16/4) whose first two differ by exactly 8. The triple is the closest thing to attribute offsets found anywhere — two offsets eight bytes apart plus a width of four — but it cannot be the record layout: the rock's pair is 48/40 against a record of 36 bytes, so either the numbers are relative to something else or they describe a different buffer. Validating that needs the loader, and three models across three families now give a fixed table to check any candidate against (item_228 stride 48 position 0,1,5; rock 36 position 0,1,2; field cliff 40 position 3,4,5)
column4: read the head numbers as record offsets

column2: Coverage tranche 6 exported (ranks 10001-12002); the plan's numeric fingerprints are not in the corpus
column3: Following the plan's priority 1: triage5k.tsv only held ~10002 rows, so it was regenerated with the same generator (sheetty.py triage, top 13000; top 20 verified identical to the old file) and tranche6.txt = the next 2000 unexported ranks. ExportTop on PLA-update-capped: 2000/2000 ok, 0 fail; the corpus is now 12 302 update .c files. The exact-number search then ran over the whole corpus in decimal and hex: the literal 30 is unfindable noise, and every file carrying a full pair (rock 0x17C/0x15C, item 0x23C/0x21C, cliff 0x184/0x164) or the triples (0x30/0x28/4, 0x20/0x18/4, 0x18/0x10/4) or strides (0x30/0x24/0x28) was inspected; all matches are coincidental struct offsets in unrelated functions (e.g. FUN_0012d200 writes bounds floats at 0x164/0x184/0x21C). Conclusion: the loader does not hardcode per-model numbers — it reads them from the .trmsh at runtime, so no literal search can find it
column4: expect the loader to contain the per-model constants

column2: The mesh/shader loader family is structurally invisible to size-ranked triage
column3: Every gfx2 pipeline loader located by string references (the bnsh/bushvt/bntx/bflyt archive loaders FUN_0012B0EC, FUN_0012C0CC, FUN_0012B1F8, FUN_0012C30C, FUN_0012C004) is a 12-99 line function and none of them appears anywhere in the 13 000-rank triage, whose large-score ordering only surfaces big functions. Tranches 1-6 therefore systematically miss exactly the family the plan needs. Two targeted exports closed part of the gap: gfx2_cluster.txt (24 functions: the bnsh loaders plus callgraph distance-2 neighbors) and trm_d1.txt (11 functions: distance-1 neighbors of the three hardcoded item-.trmdl loaders), both 100% ok. Any further coverage for the loader must be seed-driven (strrefs/callgraph/address-window), not rank-driven
column4: keep exporting by triage rank

column2: main.elf never calls the NVN vertex-state API
column3: The NVN resolver (FUN_00778570) stores ~200 API pointers at 0x04278650+8i, including nvnVertexAttribStateSetFormat at 0x04279000 and nvnVertexStreamStateSetStride at 0x04279028. Program-wide xref runs (ExportXrefs on 0x04279000 and on the table base 0x04278650) each found exactly one reference: the resolver itself. Many other slots ARE read through wrappers (FUN_0077c39c/FUN_0077ccc4/... call through 0x042788f0 = nvnProgramInitialize, 0x04278908, 0x04278a38...), so the read pattern is visible to xref when it exists. The vertex slots are not dead analysis either: no other ExeFS module carries the strings (sdk has nvnBootstrapLoader only, subsdk0 is movie, subsdk1 is the cgc shader compiler; gfx2/trsha/bnsh strings are all in main.elf). The engine therefore establishes vertex fetch state without those NVN calls — the bnsh input-signature path is the remaining candidate (dec074: attributes are 0 position, 1 normal, 3 tangent, 5 UV0, 7 UV1)

column2: D4 batch 4: resolve the import dispatch and the data relocations of update main; document the 801 PLT stubs and 100 more functions; re-review 64 earlier entries

column2: D4 final three unknowns documented from local raw disassembly
column3: The last three update-main functions left unknown after dec303 (01fda8ec, 02ee6a54, 02eea158) were documented from the local raw machine code of the update main image (work/pla/pk2/main.elf, text segment file offset = vaddr + 0x1000), decoded with Capstone and cross-checked with llvm-objdump (identical instruction counts, mnemonics and branch targets); no GhidraMCP server was used and no game content, bytes or pseudocode were published. Findings: 01fda8ec is a coherent function of 12,089 instructions with one return (its decompile failure was only the response-buffer size); 02ee6a54 is a valid 1,548-instruction function (the decompiler error is an unresolved-varnode failure, not invalid code); 02eea158 is a 5-instruction entry stub branching to 0x030049a8, and its recorded 5,816-byte body omits 312 instructions in 9 gaps that are the targets of its nine jump-table dispatches, all inside the contiguous 0x030049a8-0x0300652b range. Each summary was written from a first read, then audited: a second fresh read plus scripted re-checks of instruction counts, call-target counts, offsets, immediates and addresses cited (all passed after correcting the items the first pass had mis-stated). Operations only: no names, signatures, types or game purpose; callee behaviour, vtable and table-driven targets stay unresolved. Private summaries live in work/d4/final-three (git-ignored); the report is reports/function-progress/d4-final-three-unknowns.md. Documentation now covers 153,476/153,476 located update-main functions; this is documentation evidence only (no N2, implementation, behaviour or binary-match claim).

column2: D4 wording correction: ret-only function descriptions must say that ret reads x30
column3: Follow-up to reports/function-progress/d4-quality-spotcheck.md. In 1,286 of the 4,822 audited D4 records whose complete body is a single `ret`, the reader-written description said that no register is read or touched (for example 'without reading or writing any register or memory'). A `ret` reads x30 (the link register) to return to the caller, so those statements are read as 'no data register'; `ret` always reads x30. The git-ignored description files (work/d4/mech-rounds and work/d4/mech-b, final.json of the affected rounds, plus the stage1/author copies of 01e811fc, the literal error found by the spot-check) were rewritten by script to say 'no data register or memory' and 'The only register it reads is x30 (the link register), which holds the return address'; only those texts changed (the shared function-progress ledger carries a generic, unaffected text for these rows). No analysis_status, implementation, behaviour or match state changed; the 4,822 ret-only records are not individually re-read. Criteria for future rounds: ret reads x30; claims derived from tool metadata must be labelled as such.
